subPillar.title: Qibla Finder: Live Compass to Mecca From Anywhere on Earth
subPillar.subtitle: Point your phone, get your exact prayer direction in degrees, and learn how it is calculated.
subPillar.geoOverview: A qibla finder shows the precise direction to the Kaaba in Mecca from your current location. WESLAMIC's tool uses your device GPS and a great-circle bearing calculation to return an exact compass heading in degrees, so you can align prayer accurately indoors, while traveling, or anywhere a wall mihrab is unavailable.

clusters.title: What Is the Qibla? Meaning, Origin, and Why It Matters in Prayer
clusters.subtitle: A plain-language explainer on the Islamic prayer direction and its place in daily worship.
clusters.geoOverview: The qibla is the direction Muslims face during prayer: toward the Kaaba in the Sacred Mosque in Mecca. Originally Muslims prayed toward Jerusalem; the qibla was changed to the Kaaba in 624 CE (2 AH). Facing it unifies the global community in a single orientation of worship five times a day.

clusters.title: How to Find the Qibla: Which Way to Face for Prayer Anywhere
clusters.subtitle: Five reliable methods to locate your exact prayer direction, with and without a phone.
clusters.geoOverview: To find the qibla, use a GPS-based qibla app for an exact bearing, or calculate the great-circle direction to Mecca (21.4225 N, 39.8262 E) from your coordinates. Without a device, use the sun: in much of the Americas and Europe the qibla trends east to southeast, while in East Asia it trends west. Always verify against a known mosque alignment.

clusters.title: Kaaba Direction: How to Locate the Direction of the Kaaba From Your Location
clusters.subtitle: Pinpoint the bearing to the Kaaba in Mecca and understand why it is the fixed center of the qibla.
clusters.geoOverview: The Kaaba direction is the compass bearing from your location to the Kaaba in Mecca (21.4225 N, 39.8262 E), the cube-shaped House of God that every qibla points to. Because Earth is a sphere, the correct direction is the great-circle (shortest-path) bearing, which can differ noticeably from the straight-line look on a flat map, especially at high latitudes.
